A scientific breakthrough of this magnitude is only possible after painstaking laboratory work under the umbrella of a secure and adequately-funded research environment.

Mr. Speaker, this week is marked as National Forest Week and the opportunity is provided to us to consider how our lives are affected by Canada's forest resource.
More than 800,000 Canadians work directly and indirectly in the forest sector. I would like to pay tribute to those people who are the driving force behind Canada's forest industry, for it is their skill, dedication and professionalism that keeps forestry on the top of Canada's economy. National Forest Week should be a celebration of their commitment.
In particular, I would like to draw attention to the forest industry on the South Shore of Nova Scotia, to the Christmas tree growers, the woodlot owners, the sawmill operators and workers, the people of the Canexl plant in East River, of the Bowater Mersey plant in Brooklyn, Queens County, the forestry capital of Canada.
I congratulate all and thank them for their contribution to our life, our economy and our country. National Forest Week is for them.

Mr. Speaker, when it is lost, say goodbye.
Ironically, Canada Post's annual report boasted that the corporation focused on reliability, accessibility and affordability.
On November 1, 1989, a registered letter containing a $250,000 trust company draft was received in Ottawa by
Canada Post. By November 3, Canada Post had lost the draft. Repeated questions by the sender, addressee and lawyers have gone unanswered.
Where is Canada Post's pride and joy in operational performance? Where is the highly touted "Track and Trace System" when you need it?
When Canadians use registered mail, do they realize there is no delivery guarantee and that Canada Post assumes no liability for loss?
Canada Post admitted receiving the letter, admitted losing it, but claims no responsibility. It cost these individuals $250,000 and, apart from an initial apology, the corporation did nothing to help these people. Its mismanagement and ambiguous regulations covered the system.

Mr. Speaker, the Yukon government is leading the way once again. It has become the first government in the country to adopt the major recommendations of the 1987 Round Table on the Environment and the Economy which called for the creation of government action plans for each province and territory.
On May 7, the Yukon government released the Yukon Conservation Strategy, a comprehensive management plan to guide the use of the territories environment into the 21st century. This plan is the result of extensive public consultation with industry, environmental groups, native organizations and the public in workshops and public meetings over a period of 18 months.
The Yukon government, a New Democrat government, is to be congratulated on this progressive step. It gives us hope for the next century to see a government taking this responsibility. Let us hope that all governments, including Ottawa, follow their example.

subtopic: S. O. 31 BILL C-21 COMMONS DEBATES
S. O. 31 BILL C-21 COMMONS DEBATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Bill C-21 changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act have been well debated in this House. The elected representatives have made a decision, a decision that recognizes that we have a dual responsibility to the people of Canada, first to assist the unemployed and, second, to make effective use of our financial resources.
If we are to be able to continue to help those with a legitimate need in this country, we must first get our fiscal house in order. We need to examine every government program with a fine-tooth comb. The financing changes under Bill C-21 will contribute $1.9 billion to deficit reduction in 1990-91.
We cannot accept demands from the other place that will add to the burden on the Canadian taxpayer. The Canadian people will not accept it.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to congratulate Mary Ritchie of Porters Lake, Nova Scotia, who yesterday succeeded in desegregating the assembly line of Volvo Canada in Halifax.
After 16 years of Volvo's refusal to hire her, Mrs. Ritchie took her complaint to Nova Scotia Human Rights Commission. Yesterday, the commission awarded her $43,000, the largest award in the commission's history. They also ordered Volvo to hire her as soon as she completes her training course, and further ordered Volvo Canada to instigate an affirmative action program for women immediately.
Mary Ritchie has won a great victory for women. The Nova Scotia Human Rights Commission has shown its mettle in the ongoing battle against discrimination.

Mr. Speaker, in Canada we are proud of our political institutions which reflect a long and rich tradition of democracy. Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, there has now been a shameful departure from this tradition. Liberal senators, who are not elected and
did not receive a mandate from the people, are holding up the democratic process, for strictly partisan purposes.
Mr. Speaker, when democracy no longer works in Canada, this strikes at the core of one of our most sacred values. I am concerned, and with me my colleagues and my constituents.
I therefore invite this hon. House to express, loud and clear, its faith in the democratic system and publicly condemn those who so blatantly ignore the tenents of democracy.

Mr. Speaker, Section 95 of the British North America Act of 1867, simply states: "In each province the legislature may make laws in relation to agriculture in the province", and, further "That the Parliament of Canada may from time to time make laws in relation to agriculture in all or any provinces".
You do not have to be a Bay Street lawyer to deduce that both federal and provincial governments are responsible for farmers.
Wake up western farmers!
In the past four years, the federal government has provided 80.4 cents of every dollar spent by governments on agriculture. In Manitoba, it has provided 88.78 cents of every dollar spent.
What a shameful bunch of provincial pikers who claim to support agriculture in the provinces.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the Minister of State responsible for Seniors, are playing games with the senior citizens of this country by failing to tell them what is going on with the New Horizons program. Calls to both ministers' offices yesterday, trying to confirm the rumours that the New Horizons program has been eliminated or is facing
May 9, 1990

substantial budget cuts, did not produce any information which would alleviate some of the concerns.
The New Horizons program has been around since 1972. The program has served to make the lives of our seniors more enjoyable and, more importantly, they have been allowed to continue their contribution to society.
Why has the government not been up front with the senior citizens of this country? Why is it continuing to attack the seniors? First, the threat to de-index Old Age Security, then the clawback of pensions, and now the cuts or elimination of the New Horizons program. Where is the fairness and the compassion this government claims to have?
I call upon the government to lay its cards on the table now and tell the seniors the truth. Will the New Horizons program be cut substantially, or is it being eliminated completely?

subtopic: ABOLITION OF TOLL ON CHAMPLAIN BRIDGE
ABOLITION OF TOLL ON CHAMPLAIN BRIDGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, people say politicians don't keep their promises, but this certainly does not apply to the riding of La Prairie. After waiting for nearly six years, residents of Brossard, Can-diac, La Prairie and Saint-Lambert finally breathed a sigh of relief when my campaign promise to get rid of the toll on the Champlain Bridge was fulfilled last Friday.
Without my perseverance, Mr. Speaker, day after day since 1984, we would still be throwing tokens or quarters in the toll boxes on the bridge.
I want to thank my regional minister, the Right Hon. Prime Minister, the Hon. Benoit Bouchard and the other ministers with whom I discussed this matter. Many thanks on behalf of my 91,198 constituents.
At last, Mr. Speaker, my fellow citizens have stopped paying toll, and I must say the removal of this obligation is a major victory for equal access for all residents in my riding, whom I thank for their trust and support.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ABOLITION OF TOLL ON CHAMPLAIN BRIDGE

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian steel industry is suffering. Everyone appreciates this except for the Canadian government and one of its appointed bodies, the Canadian International Trade Tribunal.
This Canadian body ruled against protecting major Canadian steel producers, Algoma, Defasco, Stelco and Ipsco and removed anti-dumping tariffs against 11 countries.
Market conditions have worsened. These countries have excess capacity and will be looking for markets for their steel plate. Domestic demand and prices are down and Canadian steel remains ever more vulnerable.
I quote directly from the CUT ruling of May 1, 1990:
- more attractive prices in the exporting countries made renewed dumping unlikely-
In contrast, imports from the United States had significantly increased their share.
This ruling, along with the consequences of the free trade agreement, government policy on high interest rates, and the resultant high dollar are decimating the Canadian steel industry. I ask the Ministers for International Trade and Finance to finally assume their responsibilities to Canadian steel producers and intervene in this decision and a pending ruling by the CITT.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister. At a time when western farmers are facing a serious drop in their incomes, when American farmers who compete in the same markets are expecting increases, and when the American and European farmers are receiving massive subsidies from their governments, the western premiers, in a joint communique earlier this week, called on the federal government to "send a clear message that Canadian producers will not be bullied by unfair subsidies-either now, or in the future".
When will the Deputy Prime Minister respond to the western Premiers and bring forward a comprehensive and complete program to help western farmers survive and to defend themselves against these unfair subsidies? When is this government going to act?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in that same press communique, the western Premiers said that the federal government was spending too much money and that was the cause of high interest rates, the escalating dollar, and the loss of the competitiveness in the Canadian economy. I am not sure which one of those passages from the press release the hon. Leader of the Opposition would want us to adhere to.
We have said before, and I will say it again, that the federal government has $500 million on the table to help overcome the income deficiency in agriculture. That is not as much as we have provided in the past. The hon. member knows that we have provided support to the agricultural industry in an unprecedented fashion over the past number of years. However, given the fiscal restraints that we are under, we have provided $500 million plus $180 million for arrangements through the Farm Credit Corporation that could be provided, and an additional enhancement to the soil and water conservation program. The total package is more like $700 million. That is all we can afford at this particular time.
May 9, 1990

We have asked the provinces to sit down with us and design the kind of programs that would meet the multi-faceted problem that we are facing. It is a problem of drought, it is a problem of flood, it is a problem of high input costs, and it is a problem of low depressed prices.
I ask the Leader of the Opposition and I ask the Premiers of the provinces to stop copping-out, to come forward and to help us put together an attractive agricultural income deficiency plan which will meet all agriculture needs from coast to coast.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister.
Last night in his appearance before the finance committee, the Governor of the Bank of Canada said that he had made a mistake in mid-January by cutting interest rates. But he also said that his zero inflation policy will take quite a long time to produce results. He seems to be asking us to trust his judgment in this area, but we know that the zero inflation policy pursued by the Governor of the Bank of Canada means sustained high interest rates. Those are the same high interest rates are killing small business, killing farmers, and that the premiers are asking the government to lower.
Does this government support the Governor of the Bank of Canada's policy of zero inflation? Yes or no?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to remind the Hon. Leader of the NDP that inflation is a threat to the Canadian economy and a threat to lower-income people. Monetary policy and the interest rate policy which is being followed is a solution. Interest rates are not the disease but a manifestation of a problem which exists.
What the Governor said yesterday, if I understand him well, is that he will maintain this policy. That does not mean that interest rates will not come down, but we
May 9, 1990

must not expect them to come down artificially until such time as inflation comes down.

Mr. Speaker, inflation in the country has clearly resulted from the government's own policies, the policy of high interest rates, the policy of higher sales taxes, and the policy of tax cuts for the wealthy.
If this government is seriously concerned about inflation, why does it persist with fiscal and monetary policies which include trying to implement a goods and services tax which, by its own admission, will increase inflation? Why does the government persist with these kinds of policies?

Mr. Speaker, we have to react to the fact that there are inflationary pressures in the system which are influencing matters not only in southern Ontario but in many other provinces.
As the Governor indicated, when interest rates were lowered in mid-January, because of inflationary pressures the dollar went down sharply and the market was very volatile. So we need to work not only on the monetary side but the fiscal side.
The leader of the NDP referred to our fiscal and tax policies.
The government has been trying to restore the finances of the country to good health, and it has been taking strong, difficult measures to do this. It needs to continue to work on both the monetary and fiscal sides.
Also, we need to work together on the fiscal and monetary policies to make sure that there is capital available to industries, and that the government does not use it all. These two policies are far from being contradictory.

A supplementary, Mr. Speaker.
I say to the minister that capital available at interest rates that nobody can afford is hardly capital available.

Here is my supplementary, Mr. Speaker. Last night, the Governor of the Bank of Canada repeated many number of times that we had to maintain price stability and bring inflation down to zero. However, he did not make a commitment to full employment or to acceptable unemployment levels.
Oral Questions
Mr. Speaker, where is the limit to what is acceptable for this government?
How high is this government prepared to let unemployment rates go before it decides to reverse its polity?

Mr. Speaker, the greatest threat to jobs in this country is letting inflation get out of control. Our policies and the policies followed by the Governor of the Bank of Canada, which we support, are specifically aimed at controlling this threat, especially for the benefit of those on low incomes. It is imperative that we continue our methodical and systematic approach-and I am referring to the government with respect to our tax policy and the management of our finances, as well as to the Bank of Canada-to ensure that inflation is kept under control.
This is now being done. Yesterday, the governor indicated that according to certain indications the pressure was starting to drop. We cannot afford to ease up on these policies and we must continue to make sure that they are being carried out as effectively as possible and result in the kind of progress we all want.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans is well aware of the disastrous conditions facing the lobster fishermen on the east coast.
The processors are in the same boat. They are having a very difficult year due to the very low prices and inventories that exist. I know there are marketing plans being developed, but that is a future solution. The fishermen need to pay their present expenses.
Has the minister considered using the Fisheries Price Support Board to help the fishermen and the processors in order to break the depressing psychology that now exists, and if not, why not?

May 9, 1990
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand that the Fisheries Price Support Board was seized with an application in January, which was turned down.
There are no new applications before the board right now.
A week ago last Sunday, I met with lobster fishermen from the maritimes and will be meeting with my provincial counterparts this Friday in Ottawa. I intend to discuss a proposal that was submitted to me by the lobster fishermen.

Mr. Speaker, a supplementary for the same minister.
Yesterday, representatives of the Maritime Fishermen's Union indicated to us that there was nearly a $7 million inventory existing on the east coast at the beginning of the May season. That is an inventory of $7 million out of $260 million or is less than 3 per cent.
Will the minister admit that it appears the fishermen are being used as pawns in this very difficult situation and that high inventories are nothing but a hoax? What will the minister do to ensure fair prices to fishermen?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, lobster prices are market led. I do not think that anyone can relate the problem of market prices with a policy of that government. If one policy could be faulted it would be the conservation and management one which over the past ten years has led to the doubling of the landings of lobster in the maritimes and an increase in its value of 260 per cent. Our lobster fishermen have not done bad at all in the past.
This year the price is governed by the market and inventory. To put the whole thing in perspective, the inventory was $20 million when I entered this portfolio. Two weeks ago the inventory was at $8.5 million, now it is down to $4.5 million. This tells me that the marketing campaign which my colleague at International Trade has instigated in some 36 countries across the world is working. We will consider what kind of measures we can take to help the lobster fishermen in the processing industry this week.

When the minister first announced his farm aid program, he said that only new money from the provinces would be recognized for the program. On Monday in this House he said he was now crediting the provinces for some of their existing programs. Today in The Globe and Mail,-

May 9, 1990

put your money where your mouth is and deliver that money to the farmers now?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member knows very well that the government has stood behind the farmers in an unprecedented fashion, and still continues to do so.
As well, the hon. member knows that under Section 95 of the BNA, agriculture is a shared responsibility. The hon. member should also know that we have been involved with various joint federal-provincial programs from livestock, drought, to soil and water, to agriculture ERDAs, to assistance for grasshopper relief, to floods, you name it. This is not something new.
We have limited resources available. We have asked the provinces to sit down and try to work out the kinds of programs they would want to meet their unique needs. Then we can target the assistance and make it the most effective assistance possible. We have asked them to do that, to sit down with us and work out that sort of program.
We have indicated that any new programs they bring forward that could be seen as improving the income position of farmers in 1990 would be taken into consideration as a part of the plan.
It seems very simple. Unless the provinces want to totally cop-out of helping agriculture at this very difficult time, then we will have no other choice than to do something along the lines that was suggested by the hon. member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry. I might remind the hon. member that would not put cash into the hands of the farmers right now.
We are interested in getting as much cash as we possibly can into the hands of the farmers right now and we ask the provinces to join us in that regard.

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the minister of health I would like to direct this question to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs.
Oral Questions
Up to at least 1983 one of the most popular household and institutional cleansers in Canada, Lysol, relied on the Monsanto manufactured chemical, Santophen-1 as its active germicidal ingredient.
In the late 1970s Monsanto found and then suppressed evidence of the presence in Santophen-1 of up to 65 parts per billion-that is one thousand, seven hundred parts per trillion in Lysol itself, of 2,3,7,8-tetrachlorodi-benzodioxin-TCDD, the most toxic form of dioxin known.
When did the government know, not suspect, but know of the presence of TCDD in Santophen-1 and, hence in Lysol, and what steps did it take once it knew?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the hon. member's concern in this matter. He was courteous enough to send me notice of the question and I will try to answer it as best I can.
As the hon. member knows, dioxin is a generic term for about 70 members of a particular chemical family. He also knows that it was not until the late seventies or the early eighties that there were mechanisms to detect the presence of the particular contaminant that he is referring to, namely Santophen.
I can assure the hon. member that it was essentially through Agriculture Canada and Health and Welfare Canada that we were able to devise the methodology to detect this. I can advise him also that its use in Lysol was discontinued in the early 1980s, shortly after it was detected as being a contaminant and harmful. Therefore, it is no longer used in Lysol.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that the Deputy Prime Minister was able to make such good use of the research with which I supplied him. He only got a couple of points wrong.
As Monsanto's Santophen-1 was only one of the brands of 2-benzyl-4-chlorophenol in Canada, and as Agriculture Canada lists 56 pest control products containing the chemical and none have been tested by the government for dioxin contamination, will the government now move quickly-not wait for its current review to report-to test all sources of 2-benzyl-4-chlorophe-nol available in Canada for contamination by TCDD?

May 9, 1990
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to get involved in an argument with the hon. member but it is not 56. There may be 10 that have this contaminant, not 56. Those were grandfathered under the 1980 regime and they are being analysed further. When the results are known appropriate action will be taken.
I think the other contaminant he refers to is 2,3,7,8-TCDD. It has not been detected because it is in such minute quantities, that is less than one part per billion, that we do not have the mechanisms and the machinery to detect it. As it would be in so infinitesimally small quantities it would probably not be harmful.

Many Canadians are wondering the same thing. Will the Deputy Prime Minister, today, in his place, confirm that there is no intention of asking the Governor General to proclaim portions of the Meech Lake Accord on the 7 and 50 basis?

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs.
Statistics Canada has cancelled its original intention to publish monthly the effect of the GST on inflation in Canada. This was accepted procedure to the Minister of Finance and the Department of Finance for three years.
Why this sudden change? Why will the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs not admit that the reason this is being cancelled is that the government does not like the information which will go to the people and realizes that the GST will increase inflation by more than the 1.25 per cent that the Minister of Finance has predicted?

He also said that Statistics Canada will be able to provide a quarterly report dealing with that kind of question. Once again, I believe that Mr. Fellegi is well
May 9, 1990

known as being very competent and there is no reason to believe that he is wrong.

Mr. Speaker, the quarterly report will not provide the same information. The Prime Minister's chief of staff, Stanley Hart, was the first to ask in 1987 that the consumer price index be calculated without the indirect tax. Why is the government suddenly saying today that it is no longer possible to come up with that information?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology):

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I repeat what I said in English. First of all, Mr. Hart was then Deputy Minister of Finance, an excellent one I might add. Secondly, Statistics Canada regularly receives requests such as this one and assesses them according to its ability to provide the information wanted. Mr. Fellegi, chief statistician at Statistics Canada, was very clear. It is not possible to provide information on a potential difference between the actual inflation rate and that due in theory to the Goods and Services Tax on a monthly basis. However, this information can be provided on a quarterly basis, and that is what they will do. It will then be relevant.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister.
With interest rates over 14 per cent thousands of Canadians have been forced out of the housing market. Statistics show that the number of potential first-time home buyers has practically been cut in half. There are only 270,000 potential home buyers today compared to
475,000	two years ago when interest rates were 10 per cent and 11 per cent.
Why is this government shutting out Canadians from the dream of owning a home? Why are Canadians being forced to pay more than 34 per cent of their income toward housing? How much more proof does this government need before it realizes that interest rates are too high and must be reduced?

Mr. Speaker, last week the Minister of Communications lapsed into his Union Nationale glory days, suggesting that the CBC's 1968 national unity mandate had created today's divided Canada. Earlier his parliamentary secretary said that national unity mandates were the stuff of totalitarian regimes.

Mr. Speaker, because of our unique geography Canadians use communications more than any other country in the world to link us, to inform us and to unite us.
Does the Prime Minister agree that our CBC Radio and Television, with its extended infrastructure and through its programs, should continue to enable greater contact between Canadians across this vast land? Does he agree that national unity is an appropriate mandate and that otherwise he is sending a very dangerous message across this land?

The standing committee report urged that the country's regional and language solitudes come together. Without fostering that sense of identity and without fostering that consciousness there can be no unity. The horse must come before the cart.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have provided you with notice today under the provisions of Standing Order 52 requesting a debate on a matter of urgent and pressing concern.
As a member of a farm constituency I have witnessed the farm financial crisis first-hand. I have a large number of people who are communicating with me weekly on this issue.
May 9, 1990

As you are aware, Madam Speaker, on two occasions in the last two weeks members of the New Democratic Party have risen to request an emergency debate on the farm financial crisis in western Canada.
As you are also aware, Madam Speaker, this week the premiers of the western provinces who met in Portage La Prairie, Manitoba, called unanimously for lower interest rates in this country, as well as for the release of federal funds earmarked for the farm community. They said that they could not match dollar for dollar the programs that the federal government was asking them to match.
The provinces in clarifying their views on this matter sent a message to this Elouse indicating that there appears to be little room left for negotiation and that possibly the federal government may have to act unilaterally.
I believe it is incumbent upon Parliament to express its views to this government as quickly as possible to ensure that this government has adequate information from the members of this House to make the point to act unilaterally and possibly to release the funds as the provinces are now asking it to do.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerry Weiner (Secretary of State of Canada and Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)) moved
speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)
speechtext:
that Bill C-37, an act to establish the Canadian
Government Orders
Heritage Languages Institute, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Madam Speaker, it is with much pride that I open debate today on Bill C-37, an act to establish the Canadian Heritage Languages Institute.
Similar legislation, Bill C-152, was introduced in the last session of Parliament. At that time it was referred to a committee of the House for detailed examination and recommendations.
Those recommendations, and the helpful suggestions of many of my colleagues, are reflected in the bill we are considering today.
This legislation adds further substance to the multiculturalism policies of this government and to the strong commitments we have made to multiculturalism in Canada.

Madam Speaker, when the Canadian Multiculturalism Act came into force on July 21, 1988, it received the unanimous approval of all members of the House of Commons.
The Canadian Multiculturalism Act is a promise, a commitment made by the government on behalf of the Canadian people to this country's future.
The bill introduced in the House today is an integral part of this promise and reflects the hope and optimism contained in the Canadian Multiculturalism Act.

Section 3, subsection (l)(i) of that act clearly states the policy of the Government of Canada to preserve and enhance the use of languages other than English and French, while strengthening the status and use of the official languages of Canada.
I am proud to remind my colleagues of this government's commitment to official languages. They are the essential vehicles for our communication and progress as a people. We have strengthened the Official Languages Act. As Secretary of State, I continue to work with the provinces and community organizations to promote official languages throughout the country.
This bill, to establish the Canadian Heritage Languages Institute, gives substance to the spirit of our multiculturalism policy. It matches visionary ideals with concrete initiatives. As outlined in Bill C-37, the Canadian Heritage Languages Institute will facilitate the

May 9, 1990
Government Orders
acquisition, retention and use of all languages that contribute to Canada's multicultural identity.

Today, more than 70 languages are spoken in Canada. Some of them are native languages and were used well before the arrival of the Europeans in this country. Native languages are a very special part of Canada's linguistic heritage.

For this reason, I would draw the attention of all members of the House to the explicit reference to aboriginal languages in this legislation. I should note that this was an amendment to Bill C-152 proposed by members of both opposition parties, which I am glad to accept. I should also point out that the inclusion of aboriginal languages in the Heritage Languages Institute does not preclude native Canadians from pursuing the establishment of an aboriginal languages institute.

Other heritage languages were brought here by people from all over the world, people who decided to make Canada their adopted country.
Wherever you go in Canada, you will hear people communicating in languages other than French and English. Those languages are present all around us. They are a tangible and vibrant expression of Canada's cultural diversity.

Language is more than spoken words or a system of communication. It is the product of a community's past history. It is an important vehicle to transmit the culture of a community and its values to future generations.
Heritage languages enrich family life. When I was a young boy my only way of communicating with my grandparents was to speak Yiddish. I still am able to understand it and speak it quite well. At an appropriate time I might even introduce some of it into the debate.

How about now?
[Editor's Note: Minister spoke in Yiddish.]

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext: Translate it for us.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)
speechtext:
I will leave that for the record.
Without that third language, which I had learned at home, a whole world of eastern European culture would have been lost to me and, in later years, to my own children. Even more important it was a way of making contact, of reaching out to loved ones and of sharing the warmth and richness of family history.
In travelling the world and meeting family that I had never met before, some of them spoke Spanish, others spoke Romanian, others spoke Hebrew as their first language, but somehow, with Yiddish I was able to communicate and to have a better understanding of the family relationship. This was a way that the language of my heritage was very important to me in helping me understand my family roots. I know it is so for all other cultural communities.

Heritage languages are also a major economic resource. They are a tool that we can use when doing business at the international level, or in peacekeeping missions or educational exchanges. They revitalize our tourist industry by making it possible for us to welcome visitors to Canada in their own language. They are also an invaluable asset in multicultural publishing and broadcasting, on trips around the world and in academic circles. In all these fields, heritage languages serve our national interest and promote multiculturalism.

Our multiculturalism gives us an edge. It takes us beyond our homes and into the global market-place. If our trade delegations include people familiar with the languages, the values and the ways of doing business in other countries, then we have a competitive advantage.
The proposed Canadian Heritage Languages Institute will provide a new kind of support mechanism for the learning of ancestral languages.
In Canada today many languages are taught, both within and outside the regular public school system. In fact, we know that many provincial education systems have been expanding their activities in this field.
May 9, 1990

In the prairies, provincial governments support three types of heritage language learning: courses in which heritage languages are the medium of instruction, a variety of core second language courses, and community based classes. More than 41,000 children are involved in these programs. Almost 25,000 children in Quebec are also learning their heritage languages both within and outside the public school system with considerable provincial support. In British Columbia the provincial government has recently announced some funding for heritage language classes in addition to second language programs currently being offered.
In 1988-89 the province of Ontario had about 100,000 children enrolled in heritage language programs. These children were instructed in one of the 62 languages taught in Ontario. As a result of new legislation enacted in July 1988, these numbers are expected to increase considerably. The new Ontario policy requires that all school boards provide heritage language instruction of up to two and a half hours each week, when requested by the parents of 25 or more students within the board's jurisdiction.
These developments positively reflect earlier research in this area indicating the preference of many Canadians to have their children receive heritage language instruction as an integral part of the public school system. The teaching of heritage languages in regular schools ensures that they are indeed part of mainstream education activities, as they should be.
The growing importance that Canadians attach to the acquisition and maintenance of ancestral languages led my predecessor, the Honourable David Crombie, to consider the establishment of a Heritage Languages Institute.
He asked two eminent Canadians, Dr. Henry Kreisel of the University of Alberta and Dr. Michael S. Batts of the University of British Columbia, to advise on the establishment of an institute.

After much consultation across the country, these specialists discovered that the teachers in heritage language classes had little or no teacher training. They observed that they especially needed to know the various teaching methods. They also need access to Canadian material so that students can learn in a Canadian context.
Government Orders

In their research the professors found that heritage language teaching is often carried out in isolation and that teachers, even within the same language group, have little contact with each other. They discovered that there is an urgent need for networking. They recommended greater dissemination and sharing of information and resources between regions in the provinces and between the provinces. I am honoured today to open debate on legislation which will make these recommendations into law. What this legislation provides is an ambitious and challenging mandate, a mandate with one central purpose: namely, to provide a national focus for the teaching of heritage languages.
The institute will bring experts from across Canada together and direct them to the different priorities in various parts of the country. In this way, all available Canadian expertise and resources will be shared to find creative solutions to community needs. The Canadian Heritage Languages Institute will reach out to the educational and cultural communities, to the business community and to all levels of government. It will be an institution without walls, operating as a co-ordinator and a central contact point for the major areas of activity set out in its mandate: promotion, information exchange, teaching skills, materials development, networking and research.
The government believes that heritage languages are a major national resource. We believe they can best be preserved by a partnership that unites the federal and provincial governments, community groups, institutions and individuals.
As with any institution, there are financial considerations. The Canadian Heritage Languages Institute will be federally incorporated as a charitable organization. The status will give it much wider fund raising possibilities than would otherwise be possible.

The Institute will begin its work on a solid financial base. The federal government plans to give it a capital fund of some $800,000 for the current fiscal year and the next four fiscal years. Moreover, the Institute will receive $500,000 a year for its operating expenses in these five years.

May 9, 1990
Government Orders
Madam Speaker, this bill before us today is based on our past achievements and is also forward-looking. This legislation recognizes the importance of preserving and respecting our many cultures and languages. We thus enrich the life of Canadian society.

When we passed the Canadian Multiculturalism Act, this country told the nations of the world that we value our multicultural identity. We consider it an invaluable asset in strengthening Canada and in making this country a better, fairer place in which to live, a nation where all Canadians, of all origins, have an equal and fair chance to contribute to the process of our nation building.
The Canadian Heritage Languages Institute will be in keeping with this proud and visionary tradition. It will serve as a point of intersection, a crossroads, linking our many cultural communities to their own vast potential within Canadian society.
We are a people who understand what progress means and how to achieve it in real terms. There are opportunities today and every day to make progress happen, to foster a society that has fairness, equality and understanding at its foundation: a nation spurred on by a spirit of competition and committed to the cause of human rights around the world. We have made impressive inroads to date, but we know even greater opportunities lie ahead. This kind of Canada can be our generation's legacy to the children of today and tomorrow.
The Canadian Heritage Languages Institute bill is one step, but a vital one, toward a more progressive Canada for all of our citizens. It is my hope that the House will give this legislation rapid passage so that the institute can assume its rightful place as a signpost of a modem Canada, and as a sign of hope for the next generation.

Madam Speaker, I welcome the opportunity today to speak to Bill C-37, an Act to establish the Canadian Heritage Languages Institute.
The concept of legislating support for the teaching of heritage languages is not really new in this country. At the turn of the century, when the Prairies were settled, large numbers of immigrants who spoke neither English
nor French were attracted partly by the promise that their children would receive instruction in their mother tongue. At first, arrangements were made to provide for this, but towards the end of the settlement period, these provisions were withdrawn.
Sociologist Evelyn Kallen recently raised this question, saying that Canada's commitment to multiculturalism would be neither genuine nor realistic until heritage language rights were guaranteed under the Constitution. Without proposing to grant official status to heritage languages, she replied that if we are truly to respect our ethnic diversity, we must guarantee access to education in the language of choice.
A research study by Reitz, The Survival of Ethnic Groups, shows us that preserving its heritage language is more important for an ethnic group's identity and interaction than membership in an ethnic church or living in an ethnic neighbourhood or even marrying within the ethnic group. The conclusion is that the emphasis placed on language in our cultural policy by official and other language groups is, by and large, justified.
For all these reasons, I certainly agree with the principle of creating a Canadian heritage languages institute, but-there is always a but-I have serious reservations about the commitment of this government.

Madam Speaker, I would like to highlight what the Canadian Heritage Languages Institute's goals are so everyone can have a clear understanding of the proposed bill.
They are: one, to promote and develop the field of heritage language learning in Canada; two, to undertake public education, develop and disseminate Canadian-oriented learning materials, assist in the development of programs to improve standards of heritage language instruction and carry out research activities of importance to heritage language learning in general; three, to be located in Edmonton and work closely with organizations, individuals and groups from across the country. It is to consult with community-based organizations, educational institutions and the provincial territorial governments to ensure that all who are concerned with heritage
May 9, 1990

language learning benefit from the activities of the institute.
It should be managed by a board of directors appointed by the Governor in Council on the recommendation of the minister following consultation with appropriate government institutions, organizations and individuals. It will receive $6.5 million over five years from the department, part of which will establish an endowment fund to ensure its continued operation. It will be a charitable foundation which can receive financial support from the private sector and community sources and as well, from provincial and territorial governments. It will present an annual report of its activities to the minister for tabling in Parliament which will include financial statements and an auditor's report.
It will be evaluated by the minister in consultation with the board following anniversaries of the passage of the Canadian Heritage Languages Institute Bill. These are very impressive goals. Let us look at them a little closer.
Madam Speaker, how can a government that claims to listen to Canadians on the one hand have a goal of consulting them and on the other turn a deaf ear to the requests made by the organizations consulted?
The 1990 Budget showed us how important the Conservative government thinks multiculturalism is. We saw that while it talks about its commitment to heritage languages through the creation of an institute, in one stroke it cuts the very necessary funds for the schools that teach these same languages.
That is a strange way to implement objectives 1, 3 and 4, involving education, co-operation and promotion of heritage language teaching.
But maybe I misunderstood. Perhaps the objectives will only be taken into consideration once the bill is passed and for now, they are to be ignored.
Madam Speaker, the Conservative government says that it wants to help community organizations so that they can benefit from the activities of the Institute. Could the Minister of State for Multiculturalism and Citizenship explain to me how these organizations can benefit from the Institute's activities if they first have to
Government Orders
close down owing to his government's lack of commitment?
Canada is now going through a national identity crisis and this is the time the Conservative government has chosen to cut the funds for schools that teach heritage languages, nearly 1,500 schools affecting over 150,000 children and 5,000 teachers!
Madam Speaker, when I asked the minister in March why it was necessary to cut the funds, which seemed to me and still seems to me to be contrary to his policy, he answered, "Times are tough". However, going back to objective 6 of Bill C-37, we see that the Institute will receive $6.5 million. Would it not have been possible to decrease the Institute's funds a little in order to gradually reduce, instead of drastically cut, the funds for schools that teach heritage languages, thus giving them time to get back on their feet?

Madam Speaker, the cuts to heritage languages do affect unity, whatever the minister might say. We sell Canada as being a mosaic as opposed to a melting pot. The Conservative government, by oh so subtly denying individuals from belonging to their ethnic group through culture and language, does not permit these individuals to feel a part of this mosaic. Language training is essential in understanding the importance of culture, and maybe immigrant groups would have a better understanding of the French fact in Canada having had to work hard to maintain their own language.

Madam Speaker, promoting the establishement of chairs in multicultural studies in Canadian universities is to be commended. One cannot deny the importance of discovering the expression of ancestral cultures through literature, the performing arts and the plastic arts. All this is wonderful but far removed from the day-to-day teaching of heritage languages in some remote comer of Canada.
Why is this government cutting funds by $4.1 million, an amount that heritage language schools need to survive. Where did it find $14 million so that adults could get language training? Doesn't this government have strange priorities? I guess as long as it looks good and pays dividends-

May 9, 1990
Government Orders
The government is unable to find $4.1 million to maintain a long-standing heritage language teaching program, but has no problem spending $14 million on classes for business people. Would it be an investment in the next election?
Madam Speaker, I want to be perfectly clear. I am not against business people learning another language, far from it. But I am against using budget cuts as an excuse to withdraw $4.1 million, when both amounts are spent on non official language classes. Where is the logic in this?

In the news release of the Minister of State for Multicultural and Citizenship of September, 1989, the minister said, and I quote:
The need for this Institute is stronger than ever because enrolment
in heritage language classes is greater than ever. Our figures show that
there are 129,000 students enrolled in 1,557 supplementary heritage
schools across the country studying 60 languages.
The news release continues by specifying that these schools run classes outside the public school systems with as many students enjoying heritage language instruction offered under the aegis of the provincial ministries of education. Then, there is this specification which states: "All of these students should benefit from the activities the Institute is expected to undertake".
I would like to minister to tell us what happened between September, 1989 and budget day. Since when did the term "all" mean "half"? And, if one of the reasons justifying the creation of an institute was the number of students enrolled in programs. Why were the funds cut?

Madam Speaker, establishing such an institute will help us enhance the professional skills of heritage language teachers, but no attempt should be made to play the role of universities or provincial governments. Until further notice, education falls under provincial jurisdiction.
Another role of the Institute will be to prepare didactic documents of Canadian content, and this has to be done through consultation with and consideration for communities as such, and not only the intelligentsia.
These documents will reflect the Canadian reality to the extent that they relate to actual endeavours and past educational experiences. This will be one way to find out whether the Conservative government is serious, for to this day it has yet to demonstrate real interest in the survival of heritage languages and cultures.
The second aspect of the Institute's mandate will be to undertake extensive research into the learning of heritage languages in general. Again we will have to keep a close watch to ensure that the trend is not to publish papers which will end up gathering dust on the shelf.
It is far too easy to get sidetracked in research and write about lofty theories which are of no use to anyone. We in the opposition will see to it that any research undertaken is directly related to the teaching of heritage languages and that, above all, it is likely to improve the short- and long-term situation. Since the Institute is intended to be a tool for teachers, it will be up to us to make sure that it is and remains so.

Consultation seems to be a key element in the raison d'etre of the institute. If this is the case, why are aboriginal groups included in multiculturalism? Their view of multiculturalism is one that excludes aboriginal groups. They consider themselves as first people, and rightly so. Were they not consulted? Were they not heard? Or, were they not listened to?
The Conservative government said that it wished to promote heritage languages to enhance the Canadian mosaic. But, at the same time, it is ironic that in the 1990 budget cuts aboriginal people were hit so hard by the Secretary of State, that the Native Communications Program of $3.4 million was cut. It provided funding for 15 native language newspapers. They provided opportunities for work experience and enhancement of aboriginal literacy. These cuts dealt a severe blow to those seeking to preserve and promote aboriginal cultures. The natives provided funding to the Inuit Broadcasting Corporation and will affect 95 per cent of all the Inuit who watch its programming. Again, this corporation provided for the opportunity for cultural retention. Is this how the government promotes language and culture?
May 9, 1990

Government Orders
Madam Speaker, how can anyone trust a government that acts this way? A government that claims to promote Canadian multiculturalism and in the same breath destroys the bases of these cultures. Whether one closes down a newspaper, reduces funds to a radio station or cuts grants to schools for teaching heritage languages, the results are the same: denigration, destruction, and increased tensions and prejudices.
How can the Minister of State claim to be interested in the Canadian mosaic when he cannot convince his own party that it is important? How can he accept a $4.1 million cut-back in language teaching while the Minister for International Trade gets $14 million for the same reason but not for the same clients?
Madam Speaker, if we want a strong Canada, we must invest in its multicultural heritage. It is important for everyone to feel that he or she has a place in our society and cutting funding is not the way to achieve it. If the conservative government really wants to promote the Canadian mosaic in concretely and not only in theory, it must act without calculating to the penny how much its measures will bring in.
In these times of political and economical questioning, tensions build up and we look for scapegoats. We must act now! We must stop giving differences a negative value and find their plusses.
The conservative government doesn't seem to realize the importance of heritage languages in the preservation of cultures, pride and dignity. It is only when we are able to respect others with their differences that they will respect us and that we are going to build a strong Canada.
Madam Speaker, the creation of the Canadian Heritage Languages Institute could very well be a step in the right direction. I say "could" because there is a long way to go from the project to its realization. That is why we, of the Official Opposition, intend to keep an eye on the government so that, as the minister promised in September 1989, the Institute will have positive impact as much on complementary schools that will have new financial needs as on public schools. If the government really believes in the Canadian mosaic, now is the time to prove it.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I would take this opportunity to indicate that tomorrow will be an allotted day for the purpose of supply.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Weiner that Bill C-37, an act to establish the Canadian Heritage Languages Institute, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to speak to this bill, Bill C-37, an act to establish a Canadian Heritage Languages Institute for western Canada. I think it is very much needed in many respects. However, I will say at the beginning that we have some very strong reservations related to the priorities represented in this bill.
As the minister indicated earlier, this was introduced as Bill C-152 in the last Parliament. I noticed, in looking over the previous bill, that there were some amendments that I assume were made in committee, including the emphasis on the promotion of heritage languages. I noticed the addition of "and their benefit to Canada." I think that is a very important point.
Before I get into the bill itself, I would like to mention something for the benefit of certain Canadians. I can imagine some of them in Vancouver East at this moment who might cynically say: "Why do we need to be putting money into heritage language classes and a heritage language institute? Why is this important when we are short of funds? Why should we not be teaching just English or French as a second language to the many immigrants who are coming to Canada? They need this in order to adjust, become part of our society, get employment, and so on."
I agree that teaching English or French as a second language is the important language responsibility of the federal government. It is a first priority so that people can become part of Canadian society and adjust very quickly.

May 9, 1990
Government Orders
However, the purpose of this bill, and heritage language training generally, is very definitely a Canadian purpose. Let us make no mistake about that. That purpose and the goal is to enrich the multicultural heritage of Canada and Canadian citizens, both those whose parents and grandparents came from another country and those who were born in Canada of English or French heritage who may also want to study heritage languages.
In Canada, heritage languages are treated as ancillary languages, supplementary to either English or French which all Canadians should speak. In many cases, we know that it is the children and grandchildren of immigrants who go to classes on Saturdays or in the evenings. They do it as a part-time activity. We think that heritage languages are very important, particularly to immigrant families, as an enrichment and to promote family unity.
Many of the children in my riding would not be able to communicate with their grandparents, as the minister indicated in his experience, unless they were able to learn the language of the grandparents. If they do not know it when they become teenagers, there is a greater risk than ever of both poor communications and a division of cultural attitudes.
Getting back to this bill, the purpose of the proposed Canadian Heritage Languages Institute was outlined by the minister today. Also, as my hon. colleague from the Liberal side has just mentioned, it was outlined by the minister last September. As she has mentioned, it is very important to look back at that statement because it was said in a different context.
The press release reads:
The Institute, whose objective will be to encourage the preservation and use of heritage languages throughout Canada, will be located in Edmonton-It will not, however, be a location where people will go to attend classes.
A lot of people have asked about this.
Institute activities will focus on national teacher training and program development, the production of Canadian-oriented learning materials, public education and research into all aspects of Canada's heritage languages.
The press release goes on with regard to funding. I am repeating what the member just said, but it is very important. The press release continues:
"The need for this Institute is stronger than ever, because enrolment in heritage language classes is greater than ever," said Mr. Weiner.
"Our figures show that there are currently 129,000 students enrolled in 1,557 supplementary heritage language schools across the country studying 60 languages," he added.
These schools run classes outside the public school systems; there are as many students again enjoying heritage language instruction offered under the aegis of the provincial ministries of education. All these students should benefit from the activities the institute is expected to undertake.
It was a very important statement by the minister last September. He is definitely saying-I believe he was right-that the reason we need an institute is to service the front-line, community heritage language classes in 60, 70 or 80 different languages. Parents are sending their children to those classes and some adults are going as well. Their teachers can benefit from the resources that an institute would provide. However, if there are only "x" number of dollars and you have to choose a priority, which is going to be your priority? The front line classes to teach heritage languages, or this fancy academic institute in Edmonton?
It is pretty clear that the $4.1 million the government took out of heritage language classes in communities is a first priority. If we do support this bill, it will be with that in mind, that the funding for those classes must be reinstated.
It is quite irrational to think that we would be proposing to spend over $7 million, if my arithmetic is correct, over five years for this new institute, if we are refusing to fund a veiy small amount per class to the community classes which this institute is to serve. I will come back to that point.
We originally did support this bill to establish a heritage language institute in western Canada. We felt that this would balance similar services that are now available in Ontario and Quebec. We do not object to it being in Edmonton because we know that the Tory members in Edmonton need a lot of political support these days. We will support it being in Edmonton, provided that there are decentralized services available in all four western provinces and in the major centres where there are a great many of the heritage language classes. This is very important.

In the briefing that we had from the minister's staff, we were told that there would be outreach and there would be resources that would be decentralized. But there is nothing in the bill to indicate that. That is something we should be looking at in committee.
As has already been said, the institute would provide resources and training for teachers and students and improve the Canadian content in textbooks and resources. That is a very important point. I have had complaints from people who are studying Cantonese and Mandarin. The Library of Canada and many of the local libraries only have books from Taiwan. Of course, many of them, both from the point of view of the culture and also politically, do not accept that these books should be produced in Taiwan. Canadian materials would make much greater sense.
The institute would also help to improve teaching skills, provide research and so on.
I would hope that in a western institute located in Edmonton it would stress the most common languages in the heritage of western Canadians. In this way, it may be very different than the eastern institutes. Again, I will use Vancouver East as an example because it is such a multicultural community. Cantonese, Mandarin, Korean, Vietnamese, Punjabi, Hindi, Japanese, as well as Italian and Portuguese are the languages that the families in my riding need and that I would hope would be stressed in resources from the institute.
We also agree with the method of financing provided in this bill which provides an investment of capital funds, $800,000 per year, the interest to be used for operational purposes in developing programs and a further $500,000 for operating costs. That is a sensible way to do it. This would be a charitable organization which could raise funds additionally in the private sector and from individuals.
Now I come back to the crucial point of our criticism of this bill. We approved this institute prior to the recent budget. As I stated earlier, the minister had related it to local community programs last September. We felt that it was an important resource that should be funded.
However, the recent budget and the devastating impact that it has had on frontline heritage language classes in local communities is quite unacceptable. The complete federal funding of over $4.1 million has been
Government Orders
withdrawn from such programs with very little warning. This has undermined classes right across Canada. I was in Saskatoon not too long ago when this was announced. They were quite unsure of what to do. They were having to lay off teachers and close down classes. In their case, it was the total multi-language institute that they have in their own community that was threatened.
The teachers in these classes are not paid very much, and they should be paid more. They are dedicated people, usually immigrants themselves. Parents help out with the maintenance in the centres. The facilities are quite often donated so rents are not high. We are not talking about a lot of money for the number of children and the classes provided. The government must simply reconsider and reinstate funding for these community classes.
I mentioned earlier that the government has also taken money from ESL classes when they cancelled the CILT program. One wonders if the money from these two combined programs, heritage language classes and CILT are what is going into this new institute. If so, that is something that we cannot support.
The community languages classes are an integral tool of multiculturalism. The minister has stated this. They promote family unity and a real appreciation of ethnic culture. Someone once said that to eliminate language is to eliminate culture, because we transmit cultures through language.
The federal government's withdrawal of funding for community classes contradicts the minister's statement which he made and the statements he made today praising this bill. Yesterday in committee I asked the minister to give us the rationale for cutting the funding for heritage language programs in local communities. The minister said that he felt that classes could manage very well without federal funds. I know that for the classes in my community, this is not true at all. Many parents are working very hard. They have several children going to these classes. They quite often work for minimum wages, or they have a small business that they are struggling to survive in and they simply cannot afford to pay the full cost of classes.
The minister said that personally he could afford to pay for the language training he had. Well, perhaps that

May 9, 1990
Government Orders
is true in his case, but it is certainly not true for many families across this nation. It is very unfair to say that.
He also said that heritage language training should not be trivialized. I could not quite understand what he meant by that. Perhaps the minister would explain later what he meant by that. Heritage language should not be trivialized and therefore cutting funds somehow is trivializing heritage languages. It did not make any sense.
According to the Canadian Ethnocultural Council and the Canadian Coalition on Multiculturalism, recent figures show that there are 150,000 young Canadians learning 60 languages in 1,556 community schools across Canada. That means that thousands of teachers are also involved in these programs.
What a rich heritage this represents for all of us, not just for the people who are enrolled in those classes. It is an investment in our future. I am sure that the minister of trade has recognized that learning languages, particularly those of the Pacific Rim, will be very valuable economic assets and very essential to our international relations and trade. The best time to teach these languages is when children are young. We know from our experience with French and English teaching that it is far more effective at that stage. It is a small investment for such great benefits.
I have visited many heritage language schools in my riding and in other communities. I know how hard they are working and what an excellent service they are providing. We must have those funds reinstated, as I said before.
It seems most contradictory that the federal government would be willing to pay $7.5 million over five years to establish a heritage language institute as a resource centre for these community classes, when the community classes themselves are not going to be able to continue in many cases, or are certainly not going to be able to use sophisticated resources because they will probably have volunteer teachers.
The teaching of heritage languages is a fundamental aspect of multicultural policy in Canada. The Canadian Ethnocultural Council states that: "Federal funding cuts are a back tracking on the commitments that were made
in sections 5.1(f) and section 5.1(e) and 5.1(h) of the Canadian Multicultural Act".
These are the sections that deal with heritage languages and heritage cultures.
The CEC also states that this contradicts the government's intention to improve Canada's international competitive position, as fluency in the world's languages gives us an edge in trade development.

Madam Speaker, it is an honour for me to express my support for the passage of the Canadian Heritage Language Institute bill. This legislative initiative will take an important lead in introducing a new era of federal support to Canada's heritage languages.
Many language groups from across Canada have called on our leadership in a promotion of this rich and living resource. They have been highly supportive of all efforts to realize the potential of an institute. They have
witnessed the evolution of this government's commitment to heritage languages, a process marked by a new direction and application of our efforts.
We are providing leadership at the federal level to ensure that these languages continue to give expression to our multicultural character. The Canadian Heritage Language Institute is a symbol of our new approach and will ensure that heritage languages continue to make significant strides toward mainstream Canadian life.
More and more people now understand that heritage language programs are not mechanisms for fostering sentimentality. They are the life source for our cultural communities and a vehicle to transmit culture from one generation to the next. Indeed they are a genuine source of cultural enrichment for all Canadians.
The institute will match ideals with practical means to achieve them. It will promote new ways and means to ensure the use, acquisition and retention of all languages that contribute to Canada's multicultural identity. One way it will achieve this objective is through the development of better teacher training and language programs and Canadian oriented learning materials. The institute will also conduct practical research into all aspects of Canada's heritage languages.
The institute will put an end to isolated research and will place a new emphasis on applied research. Above all, it will address the practical needs of particular language groups, help to and meet these needs where they matter most: in our classrooms.
The institute will be located in Edmonton. It will work closely with organizations, groups and individuals from all over Canada to encourage the preservation and use of Canada's many heritage languages.
The board of directors will consist of knowledgeable and experienced individuals with expertise in the area of heritage languages.
The institute will tap the collective knowledge of experts from across the country: linguists, teachers, language specialists, and scholars. It will make use of the language skills and cultural understanding of individuals of all origins living within our borders.
May 9, 1990

While the institute will represent a collaborative effort, it will also play a leadership role by helping achieve nationally acceptable standards of teaching for the successful retention of heritage languages.
To be worth while our response and assistance must be timely, with a view toward future horizons. The institute will also have sufficiently broad scope to respond to contemporary challenges.
Since the institute will be incorporated federally as a charitable organization, its financial resources can be augmented by outside funds. In particular, we hope the institute will be successful in encouraging the support of provincial agencies and ethnocultural communities. The money allocated for the institute is nothing less than an investment in our cultural identity.
Charles Berlitz, the pioneer of multilingual instruction, compared living in this world and speaking one language to "living in an enormous mansion and staying in one room".
As Canadians we cannot close doors on the vast potential for growth offered by our multicultural identity. Heritage languages open a door to untold opportunities and potential for Canada.
I am proud to support the establishment of the Canadian Heritage Languages Institute as a contemporary way to promote the development of Canada's rich linguistic heritage.
I urge my fellow parliamentarians to join me in supporting this important piece of legislation as we seek to fulfil the promise of this innovative yet also truly human institution. In the long run we can be confident in the knowledge that our support to this institute has contributed to building a truly multicultural society where the needs of our people are our greatest priority.

Madam Speaker, I imagine this applause is for the opposition, and I am referring to the Liberals, before they start speaking to a subject that is very important to the spirit of this country, the soul of its people and the vision this country wants to give Canadians of their future.
When I hear people- I see my colleague from Quebec who probably thinks this subject is far too

complex for his lights. I will switch to another language unless he shows some appreciation of the subject we are discussing today.

When I think about what I heard today in this debate, I wonder whether there is a basic problem when we talk about multiculturalism and the identity of this country. I heard them talk about setting up a model for establishing that which is necessary for a valid heritage lane program, be it in the question of developing resources, be it in the question of developing materials, techniques for training teachers or for establishing national standards for the teaching of a heritage language and training teachers so that they would be able to produce the kind of work in the classroom that would reflect those standards which are Canadian.

Madam Speaker, this surprises me.

I am really surprised to hear things such as this. Recently, we heard the minister acknowledge, as we all do, that education standards in the classroom are under provincial jurisdiction. Perhaps one of the great tragedies of this country is that we do not have enough national standards for our two official languages. We are going to impose national standards on the establishment of heritage language studies.
A Canadian context for the establishment of studying Cantonese and a Canadian standard for teaching Italian. Does the minister want to establish a Canadian context for the appreciation of materials that will help in the understanding of Spanish, whether the student comes from Ecuador, from Castille, from Mexico or from Argentina?
If we are going to recognize that this country is truly multicultural, and if we really are serious about establishing a centre that fosters, promotes and enhances the study of heritage languages, then we have to be serious about the diction that we employ. We cannot on the one hand support a centre that imposes a new image of Canada that recognizes the demographic reality represented by 8 to 9 million Canadians who are of neither francophone nor anglophone origins but share a great equality that we have established in this country.
We cannot in a most condescending fashion, dictate that they will learn their language in a way that we think reflects Canada when we do not accept those same standards for establishing a milieu when studying English or French. You might remember just a few days ago, Madam Speaker, the Sorecom poll that indicated that in Quebec the residents are, increasingly, beginning to think of themselves as Quebecois.
That sends shutters of fear everywhere. As I read the rest of the Sorecom poll, it gave me an indication that one of the things that is happening in Quebec and everywhere else-perhaps this government is beginning to recognize it-with the establishment of this particular institution, is that people are beginning to take great pride in the means by which they express their individuality, their character, their aspirations and, in fact, their very existence.
Language is the soul and expression of everything that we aspire to, and everything that we live. We use it to express our emotions, the love we have for our families, the aspirations we have for our children, and to conduct our business.
I am not of English or French origin. I had to learn both languages. English is not the language that I use when I speak and communicate with my family; nor is French the one that I use when I conduct business. I really do not appreciate anyone telling me what my cultural and linguistic metropolis should be, whether it is in Edmonton by a group of academics, scholars or linguists who come together to establish a linguistic national standard for the way that I address my family, with the experiences that I have had in this country and before.
Madam Speaker, if you will permit me, in my own language-

I cannot allow another to dictate to me how I should express my thoughts, experiences, aspirations, the love I have for my family, my culture, the manner in which the history of my people developed and continues to develop, and how to express the veiy essence of my being and character. The minister will understand this, because he has given us a personal example of his

To immerse it in an institute that is teaching all kinds of languages and where the majority of the staff is not likely to be aboriginal is not

But the soul of Italian Canadians will have been extinguished in Canada. There are only about a million of us in all of Canada, and only about 600,000 in Toronto and environs. That may not be a significant figure to many people; it certainly is significant to me-just as it is significant for all Canadians to be able to use language as a means of expressing their total being and character.
I find no problem with aboriginal Canadians thinking in terms of having standards they think are appropriate, not only for the maintenance of their language but the promotion of their language, so that the spirit of their being is not only protected-and I think we have to go much beyond that-but is allowed to flourish. If it would flourish to the extent that it spills over and is then appreciated by others as a focus point not only for study but for communication, so be it.

What I do not agree with is that there is a suggestion some place that there are those who fit into the multicultural definition and those who do not. Perhaps I did not make it very clear although I tried very hard, but as far as I am concerned this country is multicultural.
