It is true that on an official basis for legal, traditional, economic needs, we use two languages. I recognize the importance of that but, if we are going to achieve total equality in this country, then we have to respect each other in the way that we express our experiences with and among each other. If, in this House, in our laws, and throughout the nation, we use French or English as the means by which we access government and justice, then so be it.
I caution the member not to think in terms of excluding ourselves from the multicultural concept. Madam Speaker, I am pleased to join members here in speaking to this bill which deals with the issue of heritage languages in our country.
I cannot get into my remarks very far without noting, for the record, the nature of the riding that I represent, Scarborough-Rouge River. It is a riding that has many new Canadians who have brought with them their own languages from other countries around the world. One of those languages is English, but the proportion of others is so great that, as I look to my own riding executive, almost everyone on it brings with him or her another language beside English. This has made us in our community stand and deal with the issue of first language, second language, and heritage language.
As we all know, this country has been founded on diversity, so much so that many of us wonder from time to time how we ever managed to bind the country together in the first place. To begin with, we have many native tongues still spoken across the country by the aboriginal community. I think it is fair to say that this is an area where the country has not paid enough attention to fostering the continuance of the native languages for our aboriginal peoples.
Culture rides on the back of language. Language is a vehicle that carries culture and, in many cases, the continuance of valid and rich native cultures is in jeopardy.
In my riding-I am sure it is true for many urban ridings-there are many languages being spoken on the street: Greek; Italian; German; Chinese, by some 30,000 constituents, both Mandarin and Cantonese; Filipino; the south Asian languages of Hindi, Urdu, Punjabi, and others; Japanese; Armenian; Spanish; and Portuguese.
May 9, 1990

My native tongue is English, and there are others who, of course, speak the other founding language, French.
Bill C-37 is intended to assist the country, its educational institutions, and its community institutions to rationalize, Canadianize, consolidate and manage the delivery of heritage language education. Why do we feel it necessary to do that? I suggest to the House that every single heritage language that we have-and perhaps I could just walk away from the word "heritage" and say every single language that is spoken in this country-is an asset.
I believe they are assets to the country in the same way that our museums and art galleries attempt to acquire and secure representations and manifestations of our history and culture. Perhaps a terrible example of that is Voice of Fire, which is not Canadian at all. We have in existence in Canada something which is not artificial and created by artifice but true and living languages which we now recognize as being an asset for all Canada. I know that we would be remiss if we did not attempt, as a country, to organize and assist in the furtherance of the teaching of those languages for all the children who will come after us.
There is a problem that we run into. We have already run into it in my riding and in other parts of the country. The public school board in Scarborough has now realized that the influx of large numbers of new Canadians bringing with them languages of birth, that is original languages other than English or French, has become a very serious problem for elementary and high schools in communities where large numbers of new Canadians settle. This becomes a very serious problem in a community that prides itself on its quality of education.
Where you have significantly large numbers of students who do not speak English or French as their first language, the school board has an obligation, if it is going to teach them at all, to provide them with additional supplementary training in the English language. At the same time, the study programs of these students is damaged severely by their inability to undertake programs in English or French as a first language. As a result, there is a real danger that in some parts of our country an entire generation of students is not receiving the standard of education in English or French needed to cany on with their lives and to be successful in Canada.
Government Orders
That is the problem we run up against in a riding where there are a lot of heritage languages.
I regard this statute as an opportunity for the country to step into the field of heritage language and to assist Canadians who have a heritage language other than English, French, or a native tongue. I suppose I should be including natives as well because they are mentioned in the bill, but they may in fact warrant special attention and I will not speak to that directly. The statute will give the opportunity to the country to get into the field and assist in consolidating the delivery of the education in those heritage languages, to set priorities, and to provide a Canadian focus. The net result will be to produce continuing generations of Canadians who will know other languages and all the value that has for Canada.
In addition, it will be at least a small step in reducing indirectly the barrier of intolerance that exists across the country in the general population to other languages and cultures. That does not mean intolerance on the part of someone who happens to be English-speaking, Frenchspeaking, or native tongue-speaking. It applies to anyone, of any culture or language, being intolerant of the language of another group or person.
By willingly and aggressively undertaking the task of locating management and finance, and the setting of priorities in the field of heritage language, we will at least in part address the need to overcome those barriers of intolerance.
While there are challenges in many urban ridings such as mine, I am convinced that a real initiative, not just a cosmetic one, that can follow implementation of a bill like this, will produce benefits for all Canadians right across the country.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have a chance to participate in today's debate on Bill C-37, an act to establish a Canadian Heritage Languages Institute. I speak with mixed feelings about the legislation.
In my constituency, there is a large variety of ethnocultural communities dominated by Italians, Sikhs, Germans, Ukrainians, Norwegians, Finns, Swiss, Swedes, and I could go on. It gives the community of Kamloops a special richness that one may not find in all communities. When it became known to the various organizations that reflect those communities, there was some rejoicing that finally we were going to take a serious step toward recognizing the heritage languages in Canada by estab-

May 9, 1990
Government Orders
lishing an institute in Edmonton to promote and encourage the development of heritage languages.
On the other hand, the interpretation of heritage language in the bill states:
"heritage language" means a language, other than one of the official languages of Canada, that contributes to the linguistic heritage of Canada, and includes any aboriginal language;
It is that particular phrase, "and includes any aboriginal language", that was brought to my attention by all the chiefs and band councils in my constituency. They said to me that in their minds their language was not one of the heritage languages and ought not to be considered alongside the various ethnocultural groups and their languages in this institute. They represented the founding languages of Canada. They settled the country of Canada, or the area we call Canada now, and settled it thousands of years ago, literally thousands and thousands of years. They had flourishing cultures, dynamic languages in terms of communication and rich, dynamic communities. To find themselves attached to an institute with a variety of other heritage languages was something they could not understand. Their languages are unique to here. The only place you will find the Haida language is in Canada.
I certainly respect the value of the institute and the promotion of languages such as Italian, Ukrainian, and so on. The point is that these languages do not live or die as a result of this institute. In Canada, they may and that is why it is so important. Over all, this is not life and death situation. However, for aboriginal languages that is the case. There are 53 aboriginal languages across Canada and only three can we identify as being safe and secure in terms of their ability to carry on. It is a real struggle for all of the others.
One of the reasons we have this struggle is that last year the Secretary of State spent $500 million on official languages, encouraging the development and promotion of English and French in Canada. And we support that, of course. But only $1 million was spent on aboriginal languages. I think we can make a case, with aboriginal languages being the founding languages of Canada, that it would not be unreasonable to expect that substantially
more money be put into the development, encouragement and promotion of those languages.
However, the situation is going to worsen now. If you look at the bill, you will notice that only $1.3 million will be spent each year on all the heritage languages which, at the moment, includes aboriginal languages. So the situation is actually going to worsen, to say nothing of the almost embarrassing announcement by the government not long ago that it is going to cut back on native communications, on native publications and the ability of native organizations to communicate with one another. For any culture to maintain itself, it must have the ability to communicate. Language is the culture. The medium is the message, if you like.
At a time when we are encouraging aboriginal peoples toward self-determination, self-reliance and self-government, when we are trying to establish in a whole variety of ways self-reliance among native people, to say we are going to cut back serious funding for native publications and native media, I thought was, quite frankly, marginally embarrassing. The native community, of course, to this day cannot believe that it is happening.
That is why the native communities are so concerned that they not be part of the heritage institute. They have some interesting support. A letter written by the President of the Canadian Ethnocultural Council to the minister responsible says the following: "On behalf of the Canadian Ethnocultural Council executive committee, I am writing to urge that the aboriginal languages be removed from the definition of heritage languages in Bill C-37, the bill to establish the Canadian Heritage Language Institute."
Here we have the umbrella organization, the Canadian Ethnocultural Council, agreeing with aboriginal people across the country that they ought to have their own institute, or their own version of institutes, or their own facility to promote the founding languages of the country so that native people can communicate among themselves.
We are simply agreeing with the Canadian Ethnocultural Council on this particular suggestion. My hon. colleague from Vancouver East made an excellent presentation. I have heard a lot of excellent speeches in this House by members from all sides, but the speech today by the member for Vancouver East must be one of the most thoughtful and compassionate speeches we have heard in this House for a long time. She pointed out
May 9, 1990

some of the strengths as well as shortcomings in the legislation before us and indicated that she wants to move appropriate amendments to improve the legislation.
She also referred to the staggering rate of illiteracy among native people, something which we should keep in the back of our minds as we consider funding for the appropriate system to encourage aboriginal languages.
I said that there were 53 aboriginal languages in the country, 50 of which are endangered. The 53 aboriginal languages are grouped into 11 language families, six of which are found exclusively in British Columbia and Yukon. The Haida, Kootenayan, Salishan, Tlingit, Waka-shan and Tsimshian languages are all perilously close to extinction. Well, extinction might be too strong a word to associate with the state of the languages, but perhaps not. They, particularly the young people taking advantage of the elders of the tribes, are struggling to develop an understanding and appreciation of and competency in these languages.
The Assembly of First Nations' Declaration on Aboriginal Language states:
The Aboriginal Languages were given by the Creator as an integral part of life. Embodied in Aboriginal Languages is our unique relationship to the Creator, our attitudes, beliefs, values, and the fundamental notion of what is truth.
Aboriginal Language is an asset to one's own education, formal and informal. Aboriginal Language contributes to greater pride in the history and culture of the community; greater involvement and interest of parents and the education of their children; and greater respect for Elders.
Language is the principal means by which culture is accumulated, shared and transmitted from generation to generation. The key to identity and retention of culture is one's ancestral language.
Those are beautiful words which I think come to the very heart of the point being made, that is, the need to have a separate initiative from the Canadian Eleritage Languages Institute to establish a foundation for aboriginal languages.
I might also emphasize the point made by my hon. colleague for Vancouver East in terms of the consultative process that went into the formation of this legisla-
Govemment Orders
tion. You know, Madam Speaker, that Bill C-37 was influenced by a consultant's report prepared for the then Secretary of State, David Crombie, back in December of 1987. One hundred and thirty groups and individuals were consulted or invited to submit briefs during the consultation process, yet only three academics knowledgeable in native affairs were consulted, two from St. Thomas University in Fredericton and one from the University of Alberta. Not a single national aboriginal representative organization was consulted in the process of drafting the bill nor was there any consultation with native experts or native groups across the country.
I think this is a gross oversight and, as a result, the government has made this woeful error of lumping in aboriginal languages with heritage languages generally. I think the minister understands the error of that decision and we will look forward, in committee, to changing this whole matter.
We would be remiss if we did not say what it is we are advocating. In the moments remaining I want refer to Bill C-269 which is an act to establish the Aboriginal Languages Foundation, sponsored by the hon. member for Western Arctic. I want to read the purpose of this foundation as set out in this bill.
The purpose of the Foundation is to facilitate throughout Canada the acquisition, retention and use of aboriginal languages that contribute to the country's aboriginal heritage by
(a)	promoting, through public education and discussion, the learning of aboriginal languages and their benefit to aboriginal peoples of Canada;
(b)	providing the public with information about aboriginal language resources;
(c)	developing programs to improve the quality of aboriginal language instruction;
(d)	assisting in the production and dissemination of Canadian-oriented materials related to the study of aboriginal languages;
(e)	assisting in the development of standards for the learning of aboriginal languages;
(f)	conducting research into all aspects of aboriginal languages;
(g)	establishing scholarly and professional links between the Foundation and universities, colleges and other organizations and persons interested in the Foundation's work;
(h)	ensuring the perpetuation, revitalization, growth and protection of aboriginal languages;

May 9, 1990
Government Orders
(i)	responding to the needs of aboriginal communities as each community is in the best position to determine what is needed to ensure the survival and functional use of its languages;
(j)	providing the funding required to enable communities to develop and control the process, resources and activities needed to promote their languages; and
(k)	undertaking any other activities in furtherance of its purpose.
I cannot imagine anything that would be more appropriate as a beginning in launching a foundation to establish aboriginal languages securely across the country.
In conclusion, we support half of the principle of this bill. We have serious concerns about the other half of the principle of the bill since it includes aboriginal languages as part of the heritage language definition.
The Shuswap nation in central British Columbia has spent a considerable amount of not only financial resources but human resources in developing their language and support literature, books and research for the enhancement and development of the Shuswap language. They have struggled on minimal resources.
I hope and pray that as a result of this initiative to create an institute of Canadian heritage languages, and through recognition by all of us that we must take a special initiative in terms of aboriginal languages through a foundation or some other course, that funding, support and encouragement will be forthcoming in the future to all native organizations which wish to enhance and expand their ability to communicate within their cultural groupings through language, both written and spoken.

Madam Speaker, I congratulate my friend on his presentation to the House. I also congratulate the hon. member for Vancouver East for her excellent dissertation on this matter.
There are a number of things about the legislation that bother me somewhat. Although the idea appears to be an excellent one, there are to be fairly massive expenditures of money. There is $800,000 to constitute the capital endowment fund and an additional $500,000 to be expended for the purpose of the institute.
The expenditures, I suppose, are to be commended except when looked at in the context of what we have just seen happening in this last budget with cuts to English as a second language and cuts to citizenship and language training. I wonder what good a heritage language institute will be if there is no money for heritage language classes.
Section 10 of the bill sets out very nicely that the chairperson and the other directors shall be paid such fees for their attendance at meetings of the institute and for work performed for the institute as are fixed by the Governor in Council. We have no way of knowing what this will be. I am looking at these expenditures of money at a time when there are cutbacks. Although the idea is a good one, I would suggest that there is some hypocrisy in the government setting up an institute at a time when it is cutting out other programs that help in the binding of this country together as a mosaic.
We have often heard some very good ideas brought in with much fanfare, but as soon as the government gets the program instituted it seems to run on the rocks of the finance department's shoreline and the good idea sinks on those rocks. Does my friend have any comments comparing this program to other programs in the past that started out as a good idea but, because of funding cuts by the Department of Finance, were scuttled?

Madam Speaker, I appreciate the question. I suppose it is a matter that is on the minds of many people watching or listening in, who are concerned about how serious are the government's intentions of proceeding with the heritage institute and supporting aboriginal languages.
This is no reflection on the minister-I am certain that the minister is sincere-but I do remember on a number of occasions the huge fanfare and announcements about the Polar 8 contract for British Columbia. Finally, after all sorts of promises, fanfare and so on we were to have this Polar 8 icebreaker built which would provide jobs. It was to be a symbol of British Columbia. I notice my hon. friend from the Fraser Valley is here. He will remember those days. We all felt proud that finally British Columbia was going to get something. I remember bands playing, people cutting ribbons, fireworks, and everything else.
May 9, 1990

Then of course nothing happened; it all fizzled out. The government said: "We are sorry. We have changed our mind. We cannot do that any more". British Columbians felt as though someone had jammed a dagger in their stomach one more time. We are looking like a pin cushion out there. We are getting jammed and jabbed all of the time.
My friend is absolutely correct to ask whether the government is serious this time. It sounds good. On paper it is a great idea. I guess we will just have to wait and see. It is easy to say all these things, but of course the commitment must be there financially to make it work.
When I see the government cutting back on native publications, language training programs for new Canadians, and ESL courses in the west, I just wonder how serious the government is in its commitment to the development and encouragement of heritage languages. I can only assume by its actions that it is not serious. Let us hope that there has been an enlightenment, a change of mind, and that as a result of this legislation today the government will start putting its money where its commitments are verbally.

Madam Speaker, it is a pleasure and a privilege to stand in support of the principle of this bill.
The establishment of a Heritage Language Institute is certainly a step in the right direction of supporting our commitment as Canadians to a multicultural society and to something which has been happening at the grassroots of Canada for many decades now, that is teaching young people in particular whose families come from a different cultural background based in a different language how to speak that language, how to relate through that to the culture of their family's origin and how to relate through that to other parts of the world and other peoples of the world.
As we all know, as we face a changing global economy, as we face the tremendous challenges of the global environment, as we face the challenges of learning to live peacefully together on this earth, the ability to communicate with and relate to people all around the globe becomes an increasing strength, not only for an individual but for a nation.
That is what many people who have come to Canada over the generations have done. That is the foundation
Government Orders
they have built for Canada as a nation to play a stronger role on the globe and to play a stronger role in some of the major issues confronting the world in the next decade and indeed in the third millennium.
The institute is intended to support, as I said, what has been happening throughout Canada for decades now and for well over a century in the case of some language groups, that is the teaching of heritage languages and all that goes with it. It is for that reason that in rising today to comment on the bill I cannot avoid commenting as well on the fact that it raises some spectres of empty promises and empty shells of institutions when in the same year that the government brings forth this bill it has also obliterated any direct federal funding for heritage language programs.
I met recently with perhaps 60 people in the national capital region. Where better to represent the essence of Canada? These were people represent over 50 schools where heritage languages are taught in this region. I want to mention a few of them because I think it is important that people know the richness and wealth of different cultural backgrounds that exist in our communities, not only here in the national capital region but across Canada.
We have schools teaching Armenian, Arabic, Lebanese, Bengali, Hebrew, Yiddish, Aramaic, Jamil, Spanish, Czechoslovakian, Mandarin, Lithuanian, Dutch, Finnish, German and Urdu. We have schools teaching Greek, Hindi, Hungarian, Italian, Khmer, Laotian, Portuguese, Malayalam, Vietnamese, Japanese, Korean, Ukrainian, Punjabi, Filipino, Persian, Polish, Russian, Italian, Swahili, Sinhalese, Tulugu and Ibrkish.
We have a wealth in this country, a microcosm of the entire globe. The idea of supporting the continuation and enrichment of that is certainly one deserving of our support. Yet the people with whom I met and the people across this country who are in their own communities, their own schools and their own churches, in whatever place they can find to teach their children through the second, third and fourth generations the language of their family's origin, are concerned about whether they are going to be able to carry on those programs as effectively as they might.

May 9, 1990

The programs that are going to be most affected by the cut in funding the government has delivered this year are the smallest programs with the smallest pool of parents, families and community to draw on to support their schools. These are not schools that have ever been supported just by government. They have been supported by the communities, the families, and the businesses in those communities.
Those communities that are the poorest-and that often means the ones that have most recently arrived in Canada-absolutely need the kind of funding they are getting. They really question whether it is more important to continue the funding of the actual teaching of the languages than to fund an institute.
The smallest communities-and again those are often those which are newest to Canada with the least base to draw on-are those that are going to suffer most. Many of them are concerned about whether they can continue their program or will have to start charging fees such that the parents will not be able to afford them.
The newest schools, those that are just starting out of communities which are just getting established in Canada or have just reached a critical mass where having a school is a real possibility and which have all the start-up costs, are the ones that are deeply concerned their programs are going to be hurt by the funding cut that has hit them this year. They too question the priority of putting money into the actual teaching compared to the priority of putting money into an institute.
There is basic funding through the provinces for the teaching at heritage language schools, but that provides only a bare minimum. It does not provide enough to create a school. That is why there is such deep concern about the diversion of funding away from these programs. It does not provide enough to introduce the cultural element that keeps young children in school on a Saturday morning when all their friends are out playing, for three and sometimes four hours. The diversity of activities that teach them the language is what makes it meaningful for them, rather than just the book learning.
It is the federal funding that has provided those extra things which go into making a school and making a total cultural experience of the language. It is the federal funding that has allowed them to buy the books, the videos and all other things that go into a complete
program. It is that which has allowed them to pay their teachers more than a bare honorarium, to avoid charging excessive fees to the parents, and to bring in all those extras that make a school function.
The people who run these heritage language schools talk to me about what they feel they contribute to their community, to the broader Canadian society, through their schools. They talk, as well, about how the schools are important in their integrating into Canadian society.
There is one school in my riding which is a virtual United Nations. It is wonderful to see. The children have over 27 different languages, most of which have been learned through their heritage language schools. They know their culture and they have learned that with the help of federal funding over the years. They are sharing that with other young people. They are building in other five, six, seven, eight and ten-year olds an understanding not only of their own backyard but of the world. They are building bridges between cultures right there in their classrooms, in their playgrounds, and in their social life with their friends before and after school.
They are making an invaluable contribution, not only to the personal experience of their fellow students but to what those other students bring to Canadian society, bring to their adulthood, and bring to Canada's role in the world.
Their schools also serve as a useful bridge in other ways between the broader society and the members of the family who are slower to integrate and slower to learn the language, and that often means the woman in the household who may be home looking after the children, who may be in a job to earn extra money to support the family where her learning of the language is hampered and where she simply does not have the opportunities that other members of the family have to learn the Canadian language. The heritage language schools become for the mothers and for other people in the community another bridge integrating them into Canadian society while they retain their own unique identity.
That is why the schools are concerned that at the same time as we are building and funding an institute we are cutting back the funding to the very heritage language teaching that the institute is supposed to support. They really question not whether the institute is a good idea but whether they are going to get the institute at the

expense of the very programs the institute is supposed to assist and to enrich.
I will just refer in my last couple of minutes to what are the objectives of the institute. The first is the learning of heritage languages. We do not need an institute for that. For nearly 200,000 children across Canada that is already happening.

Madam Speaker, I was referring to the objects and why there is some concern that this institute
Government Orders
not replace heritage language teaching across the country as it seems to have done in this budget year.
The institute has as one of its objectives to provide the public with information about heritage language resources. It can only do that to the extent that those resources are also supported and continued.
It also intends to produce materials for teaching. One of the problems is that it has been federal funding that has gone traditionally to the heritage language schools which has provided the extra funds we need to purchase those materials. They are a little sceptical about an institute providing materials for them which they concede are badly needed materials with Canadian content, materials that can be more easily acquired at a more reasonable price, but if they have no money to buy them, then those materials do not do them an awful lot of good.
While I personally agree and support the principle of this bill, I caution the government against thinking that funding an institute, or for that matter a department of multiculturalism, in any way replaces its obligation to fund the very programs in the communities at minimum cost to society. These programs are carried out by the communities themselves, with only a bit of support from the government.
This institute in no way replaces that obligation. That message is clear from the groups and schools I have spoken to. I deliver that message now to the minister.
I am certainly in support of the principle of the bill, with some of the provisos that have been mentioned already by previous speakers on the bill. But we are not finished yet with the funding for heritage language schools.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Cadieux (for the Minister of Justice) moved
speechtext:
that Bill C-39, an Act to apply federal laws and provincial laws to offshore areas and to amend certain acts in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
Mir. Rob Nicholson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada): Madam Speaker, I would like to thank the other members of the House who have co-operated to help move this important piece of legislation through the legislative process.
The Canadian Laws Offshore Application Act provides for the application of all Canadian law to the offshore and it is designed to reflect the sovereign rights and jurisdiction given to Canada by the modem Law of the Sea.
In preparing this legislation, the government has had three fundamental concerns in mind: legal certainty, Canadian sovereignty and co-operation with the provinces.
Before beginning with the issue of legal certainty, a few words of background about the concepts of international law that we are dealing with here will help bring the legal problem into clear focus. The bill is concerned with the application of Canadian law to installations on the Canadian shelf.
The general presumption is that Canadian law does not apply beyond the territorial limits of Canada unless there is some specific and express indication that it is intended to have such application. This means that there could potentially be serious questions about the applicability of Canadian laws to areas that are under our resource jurisdiction, but that lie beyond the 12-mile limit of our territorial sea. This is obviously a legal question of great importance. Bill C-39 is designed to remove this uncertainty.
The second of the three objects I mentioned a moment ago is the strengthening of Canadian sovereignty. The bill reflects our sovereignty concerns in a number of ways. Sovereignty is secured through the effective exercise of national jurisdiction, which is precisely what we aim to achieve by establishing a comprehensive legal
regime in the offshore through the application of Canadian laws.
Another of our basic objectives is co-operation with the provinces in the context of offshore development. This is the spirit that has given birth to the Atlantic Accord and the Canada-Nova Scotia Accord, and it is the spirit that animates this legislation.
We have taken great care to ensure that the legislation is entirely neutral and non-prejudicial with respect to those provincial offshore claims that remain unsettled at this time. You will note, for example, that Clause 3 vests offshore rights and interests in Her Majesty in right of Canada. But it does so only with respect to areas that lie outside the limits of any province.
In addition to applying federal laws offshore, the legislation will establish a basis for the application of provincial and territorial laws to offshore areas outside the provinces and territories.
Clause 7 of the present bill will allow for the application of provincial and territorial legislation to the offshore on a more general and comprehensive basis. I should think that this provision will be especially useful in the context of ordinary private law matters such as contracts and tort claims, where we have no body of federal law that can be applied.
We recognize that the provinces and territories will want and expect consultations on the application of their laws to adjacent areas outside the provinces and territories.
Clause 7 will be proclaimed in force separately for each province or territory and each proclamation will require 60 days advance notice in The Canada Gazette. These requirements are designed to guarantee an opportunity for full consultation with each province or territory-
I would like to bring to your attention, Madam Speaker, a consequential amendment made necessary by the introduction of this bill. I attach particular importance to the application of our criminal laws to offshore activities. This will be accomplished both through the general provisions of the bill and through a series of amendments to the Criminal Code.
At present, with some exceptions, the code applies only within the territory of Canada and on Canadian
May 9, 1990

Government Orders
ships and aircraft. We consider it essential that offences on installations operating on the continental shelf and under our jurisdiction should be be able to be tried in Canada.
The Criminal Code amendments will mean that our law will now be applicable to offences committed by a Canadian beyond the territory of any state.
I would like to point out that we have simplified and replaced provisions dealing with the world-wide application of Canadian criminal law to Canadian flag ships.
Finally, to complete the package, the legislation provides that the jurisdiction of the courts, federal, provincial and territorial, will extend to installations on the continental shelf in the same manner as if they had arisen on land. This, again, will eliminate the jurisdictional uncertainty that has been apparent in a number of decisions over the course of the last few years.
Madam Speaker, I take pleasure in asking the House to support this bill.

Madam Speaker, first, let me thank the hon. member for Moncton for trading places with me tonight so that I can make my brief intervention and attend to the other business that we all have to do around this place.
Let me say at the outset that the member for Niagara Falls has clearly indicated the purpose of Bill C-39, and I will not go into that.
I would like to indicate that my caucus is in support of this legislation. We welcome the fact that the government has finally produced a bill that purports to protect Canadian sovereignty. It follows a steady stream of initiatives that have seriously eroded our control over our own destiny-the free trade deal, gutting foreign investment review, cutting the Polar 8, and acquiescing time and time again to U.S. foreign policy. It is nice to see the government moving the other way just for once.
We do have some concerns with the manner in which the legislation is to be implemented. For that reason we want to see the bill go to the legislative committee to deal with a number of questions. They are not major items. However, we think the principle of the bill is sound. It is to extend our jurisdiction in a number of ways beyond our 12-mile limit.
For example, we are concerned with the power that this bill gives to the Governor in Council. We need to know just what effect this bill would have to whole new areas that suddenly fall under provincial purview, for example, collective agreements, environmental laws, safety standards and labour laws.
It would appear that with a stroke of a pen-I realize it is not quite that simple-that Cabinet can switch on or off provincial or territorial laws in a particular offshore area at a whim. We want to be sure about the ramifications of those matters.
In terms of its application of provincial and territorial laws, the bill may in fact give additional powers to the federal government to control the tax, royalties and resource revenues that are currently going to the provinces. We want to make sure that that is not the case.
We would like to know more about how Cabinet may suspend the operation of certain labour standards to make an area's economy more attractive to large employers-in other words a federal version of the Miche-lin bill in terms of Atlantic Canada.
We want to know what the effect will be on the day-to-day lives of the people who work on the offshore, be they riggers, fishermen, sailors, or what have you.
We are concerned about the lack of appeal over and above the 60-day notification in The Canada Gazette. Because of the far-ranging nature of the kind of regulations that may be made, we are not sure that 60 days is an appropriate period of time.
These are the kinds of things that will be around for quite some time and have a major impact. Perhaps a period of 120 days or longer might be considered.
Finally, we support the principle of the bill. We welcome it. We wonder why it took from October 2 of last year to get to second reading. I notice in the draft paper that the House leaders are reviewing that it is not even on the agenda for completion of third reading by this summer. I question the government's commitment to move quickly on this matter. Certainly, we need the review of it but we are quite prepared, providing that we get satisfactory answers, to continue to support the bill and to move for its enactment as soon as possible.

Government Orders
I again thank my colleague for Moncton for trading spots with me. I thank the member for Niagara Falls for his intervention as well.

Madam Speaker, it is a pleasure to rise and speak to Bill C-39.
Our party, as well, supports this bill going to a legislative committee. We see that the bill has some definite progressive implications in the area of Canadian sovereignty, the application of federal and provincial laws and with the Criminal Code amendments.
As we see it, the bill is an attempt by the government to assert Canadian sovereignty over the Arctic and in our offshores generally, and it updates our laws in order to take into account the increased jurisdiction of coastal states under the Law of the Sea.
It sends a clear message to the international community that international waters and territorial seas are definitely part of Canada's concern. For that reason we support it.
It also confirms that the reference to internal waters or territorial seas includes a reference to the airspace above and the seabed and subsoil below. Those are important matters and issues to be considered.
It also takes into account the growing importance of the Arctic and the oil and mineral rights and assets of which exist there, something which we are most supportive.
As well, the bill recognizes that no longer can oil rigs be considered, but also other areas like production platforms, subsea installations, pumping stations and the like. These are all very positive aspects.
We are also pleased to see the Criminal Code amendments which allow us to have some hot pursuit and search, arrest and seizure provisions on the international seas as well as in our own waters.
It also makes Canadian laws applicable against Canadian fisheries in Canada and allows Canadian fisheries officials to carry out their duties on foreign vessels which, again, we see as positive.
I should say that we are looking forward to it going to the legislative committee. It needs detailed study, obviously in the area of the discretionary powers that are given to the Governor in Council.
There are concerns that the provision of the bill may subsequently be compromised or altered by regulation which can cause us some problems. It is essential that we have a very detailed study at the legislative committee stage.
This legislation looks at a new frontier, new definitions, and new players. It is very far-reaching in the areas of energy policy, environment, the Criminal Code, as well as natural resources such as fish and the like.
We are supportive of the bill. We will have other comments to make when the matter is before committee.
